subject: Art & Design
title: Critique vs. Criticism: How Designers Give Feedback
description: A fast breakdown of Critique vs. Criticism: How Designers Give Feedback for builders.

hook.text: 'I don't like it' is criticism. 'The hierarchy is unclear because...' is critique. One helps; one doesn't.

buildup.text: Design critique evaluates work against objectives: does it solve the stated problem effectively?

discovery.text: Good critique names the specific issue, explains why it matters, and suggests a direction — not a solution.

twist.text: The designer receiving critique must separate their ego from the work. The design isn't them.

climax.text: Companies with healthy critique cultures ship better products. Silence kills quality faster than harsh feedback.

punchline.text: Critique isn't about the designer. It's about the design.

quiz.question: What distinguishes critique from criticism?
options: Critique evaluates work against objectives with specific, actionable feedback

details.summary: Design critique is structured feedback focused on whether a design meets its objectives, not whether the reviewer likes it. Professional critique separates personal preference from functional assessment, using specific, actionable language rather than vague reactions like 'I don't like the blue.'
details.whyItMatters: Design is subjective but critique must be objective. Learning to give and receive structured feedback is essential to professional growth and prevents design decisions from becoming battles of personal taste.
takeaways: Critique assesses whether designs meet objectives, not taste
Professional feedback is specific, actionable, and objective
Structured critique prevents battles of personal preference

faq.question: How should you structure a design critique?
faq.answer: Start by restating the design's objectives. Assess whether the design meets them. Identify strengths before weaknesses. Frame feedback as questions ('Does this hierarchy guide the eye to the CTA?') rather than commands ('Make the logo bigger'). Always tie feedback to project goals.

faq.question: How do you handle 'I don't like it' feedback from clients?
faq.answer: Redirect to objectives: 'What specifically feels off? Does it not serve the target audience or communicate the key message?' If subjective preferences persist, reference the design brief. Anchoring discussions in documented objectives prevents feedback from devolving into taste debates.
